kids.text: Hey everyone, so my last official news posting on Openthrone.dev "Closer to a reset", on August 3, 2024 where I was excitedly talking about combat changes, recruitment fixes, and getting closer to something we could reset and actually play. The goal was to introduce the balances that plagued both earlier revisions of OT, while also tackling some issues we've talked about from DT.
And then.... I disappeared for two years.

I left OT in a state with attacking disabled, spying broken, and a server that kept crashing. People had put time into the game and the community, and I just left them waiting. There was a lot of excitement and then I just dropped the ball completely and let that die in the void.

While away, there continued to be a lot of work happening in the background. I continued to tackle what I thought was an issue, continued to try to bring a vision to life, and tried keeping the dream alive, but a pile of commits doesn't erase the silence, and an updated alpha isn't the same thing as a finished production release. So first I wanted to give a real and honest version of what happened, what has changed, and what I'm trying to do next.
Nunos has been the absolute unsung hero of this project.

He kept checking in on the server, kept talking in discord, kept the dream alive while I wasn't there. I've abandoned him the most along with the project, and somehow he has remained an absolute G. I don't think there's any amount of "fake men" that can be given to really show my appreciation for that.

OT still having even a shadow of a community to come back to is not just my doing. Nunos, thank you. And to everyone who stuck around, checked in, or kept hoping something would happen: thank you too.

Originally, I wanted to be part of a community project around DarkCurse. OpenThrone grew out of that same desire: be part of the old DarkThrone community, build something with other people, hopefully find collaborators and maintainers to work with, and bring back the kind of game we cared about.

Development started as most did in the early 2020s, late nights trying to code an idea, weeks troubleshooting it, think it works and is ready for release, let everyone play test, and then rinse and repeat the dev cycle. With AI coming onto the scene in the early days, ChatGPT.com started taking a good portion of questions I had, but the technology was (and still is) pretty flawed. It's weird when in comparison today, but trying to talk to an chatbot that could barely hold any context, spat out fun "ideas" with zero implementation effort, it was a nightmare.

We didn't have the original DT code to reflect on, we didn't have an original system to test against, we had our memory, vibes, and an idea. After time though, when the idea just wasn't working, I couldn't find other collaborators or maintainers, and AI was the smartest idiot in the room, I started drifting away. The math and the complexity of the vision were where I kept getting stuck. I was chasing a vibe and not anything concrete. I'd have an idea for how the game should feel, then struggle to turn it into rules that behaved sensibly once actual players got involved.

Trying to solve that while also keeping up with community support compounded my frustration. That was a problem with how I was managing the work, not a problem with people asking for updates. Eventually, I moved development private so I could focus without getting lost in the noise. First by checking in less on discord and really just coordinating efforts with Nunos, and then as time went on, even less time doing that.

While moving to more private development helped me work through problems, it was also a double-edged sword: I shut out the community I had wanted to build with and left me without any accountability or deadline to meet. While I think it was a good choice to change up my development process, turning my back on being transparent and working with everyone was shitty and dumb.

Meanwhile, LuK stepped up with DarkThroneGame.com, with Old Skool Gaming, and put work into his own spiritual successor to DarkThrone. I've checked in from time to time, and I enjoy what he's done. Keeping one of these games going takes a lot of effort and commitment, and I hope to see his project prosper!
I though, still had an itch to scratch with OpenThrone and I knew I needed to get back to it.
OT is now backed by AIOX
OpenThrone is now operated, funded, and hosted by AIOXperts IT Solutions LLC, my IT company.

That matters because the project is no longer relying on the same hobby arrangement as before. AIOX can provide the running project with funding, hosting, and room to experiment while I build a more mature development workflow. The code remains freely available and opensource, but now I have the support of what already powers my day to day, to help bring this project alive.

Running and managing OT was always intended to be a free-to-play cousin of a separate, more ambitious commercial game. That project was originally blockchain-based, built around decisions, actions, and even inaction having meaningful consequences. If you don't remember, a lot of this kicked off back during blockchain's 2nd wind post covid, and i still think it has a purpose but without all of the "get rich" hype that the CryptoBros were pushing. I always wanted a game that was built to be long-running, transparent, and able to grow outside of the footprint of itself. Whether that vision ever comes to be still remains to be seen.

That does not mean OpenThrone is becoming a blockchain game. OT remains its own free-to-play, open-source project for the community. Like everyone else, the intent is for OT to be a successful base project so that anyone in the community can take it and build their own ideas off of it. That is why AIOX sees the success of OT as an important one, not directly financial but as the bones for AIOX's own future ventures.

Working on OT also lets me build and try tools needed for that larger project. The AI workflow is much more mature now: more context, codebase-aware investigation, smaller concrete tasks, independent reviews, and actual verification instead of just asking for a clever answer and hoping it holds together. I get to spend more time play testing, more time scaffolding ideas with pseudocode and developing better A/B tests with results that finally matter.

The commit history covers considerably more than a new coat of paint: combat and balance work, spying, army training, banking fixes, alliances and messaging, notifications, account flows, era handling, and staff tools. There has also been work on API protections, background processing, and performance.
The useful question is what any of that means when you play.
A UI that feels like OT

In that August 2024 post, I said we still didn't have a designer and my UI skills were limited, and that is still very true. I always stated "I'm a developer, not a designer" and my UIs almost always look like they were created by an dev. So while the original OT designs worked in a lot of places, it didn't have a strong identity. I'd say it sat somewhere between "this is what I THINK DT looked like" and "that's a good wireframe for how DT would look today".

Some of that was deliberate though, I didn't want to include AI generated art in the repo, as I wanted as much of the opensource nature of the repo to feel clean. So I started opting for using my R2 buckets to store AI art to add some life to the visual, while making the code stay agnostic. It worked-ish.

The new Era 2 update has a much more deliberate dark-fantasy presentation: better race-themed artwork, framed panels, clearer navigation, a proper kingdom ledger, and more consistent army and battle screens. Mobile navigation, responsive layouts, keyboard accessibility, and the English, Spanish, and German interfaces have also received attention. The code base is still intended and works well on its own, but now we have depth and life added to the pages.
The official OpenThrone production homepage before the newer alpha design.
The updated OpenThrone alpha homepage with its dark-fantasy design and race-themed artwork.
Combat: clearer rules and consequences we can tune

That last official news posting described deciding the victor through an Offense-versus-Defense comparison while the current development engine still has an attack-versus-defense pressure check, but much more happens around it. The original goal was to make sure that attacks made sense, and prevented things like we experienced in DT:

PlayerA has all Workers + Defense units
PlayerA untrains their workers and defense units, and trains large Offense army
PlayerA then attacks PlayerB to pillage and cause massive damage
PlayerA then untrains all Offense units and retrains their Workers + Defense army

style.font: ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, Monaco, Consolas, "Liberation Mono", "Courier New", monospace

kids.text: Even worse than this though, was the fact that PlayerB could just have a huge Worker + Defense army, maybe while they wanted to generate Gold, but otherwise they could go fully Offense only when going on a period of inactivity and only their Workers would be at risk.

So the first mitigation I had added was to change up how damage and kills would spill over. If you didn't have enough Defense, then your Offense would jump in to help. Offense units were kneecapped so you weren't getting your full force's capabilities, but it meant that you couldn't just leave your gates wide open and not risk anything. If the enemy breaches the gate, then the units there should be expected to help out, though with low capabilities as they're not inherently ready for defense.

After that battles were updated to simulate alternating attacker and defender phases, up to the ten turns allowed. During each turn there's an attack phase and there's a defense phase. In addition, since we have Melee units and Ranged units, it made sense to have Ranged phases added in as well. 10 turns use to mean more damage, pillage, and death, but now also includes a fatigue rating to impact how the attacks are being carried out.

Casualties are now also tied to a replacement capacity, not just some percentage of whoever happened to be standing there. Under the current baseline tuning, a single battle's casualty ceiling is bounded by the smaller of 8% of the population at risk and five days of calculated replacement capacity, before additional limiting factors are factored in. The replacement capacity is based on the maximum number of citizens that one is able to get in a single day, which has historically been 250 + your housing level's daily citizen generation.

For example, 1,000 people at risk and a replacement capacity of 100 per day gives a base ceiling of min(80, 500) = 80. That is a ceiling, not a prediction that every battle kills 80 people. Fort protection, battle length, unit-stack limits, and other constraints still matter. Some battle casualties become recoverable wounded rather than permanent losses.

style.font: ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, Monaco, Consolas, "Liberation Mono", "Courier New", monospace

kids.text: Loot has limits too: a current per-attack cap of up to 22% of on-hand gold, with fort condition affecting what can be taken, and a separate daily pillage cap. Repeated attacks also interact with accumulated defensive pressure. These are attempts to make attacking consequential without making one bad encounter or a dogpile automatically erase an account.

Those numbers are tuning values, not sacred rules. The important change is having a coherent model we can inspect, simulate, and adjust. There is now substantial balance tooling for exploring population growth, progression, and combat over simulated seasons. It helps find problems; it doesn't replace players finding ways to break the game.
Growth and the first proper era (though...named Era 2)
A few important policy changes deserve their own section rather than being lost among combat formulas.

Auto-Recruit is being retired for the time being. In my opinion, the Auto-Recruiter was just something to mitigate the desire for all of our old Clickers in the past, but recruiting as is really needs an overhaul. The way I see it, DT used Recruiting as more of an Ad-Revenue than a game mechanic. Sure it help you get an increase in citizens per day, but it was at the expense of spamming recruit links which didn't lead to game growth, and it incentivized illegitimate means to auto-recruit. I want there to be better ways to gain citizens, and maybe we can reuse the Auto-Recruiter for Alliances instead (within reason). For now, however, we're disabling it.

Era 2 will have a bonus of 100 citizens per day for everyone, regardless of Housing level. Since we're removing the auto-click, we're going to give 100 citizens to everyone in Era 2 per day in addition to what's provided by Housing. To receive the 100 citizens, you must have been active in the previous 24hours, so login daily, repair your fort, train your citizens, etc.

There's no premium status for the first era yet. Premium is something I envision for the future, not a benefit I'm giving some players for this era. I want there to be a value to provide a premium user, and right now there's just not. If we do a Premium status, like DT Legends, it'll have a free component to it as we test out the features and ideas. We may give it to weekly stat leaders, reward random active players, etc.

Daily quests are being tested as another source of XP, gold, and citizens. That's experimental work, not an announcement that a complete quest system is already live. Keep an eye out for future announcements on this.
OpenThrone remains an open-source community project. Moving development private for a stretch did not mean I intended to turn OT into closed-source software.

There will be times when OpenThrone.dev runs a development branch ahead of the base release. That gives us somewhere to try work that isn't ready to hand to everyone running their own server. AIOX can absorb the operational impact of those experiments rather than pushing it onto community operators who are running forks.

Those development branches will also be released for people who want to self-host the cutting edge and accept that tradeoff. That is the intended approach, not a claim that every private branch is already published today.
The separate commercial project, OpenThrone.dev, doesn't change any of that. The OT project is still OT, and it should be possible to contribute, inspect the rules, and run your own version.

If you come back, tell us what doesn't make sense. Bring the awkward battle results, the confusing screens, and the numbers that look wrong. If you want to contribute, the community and the code are where that starts.
I wanted OT to be something we built together. I lost sight of the “together” part for far too long.
It's good to be working on it again. Now I need to be present for the people playing it, too.
